examples: This isn't the right address.
Isn't it strange that nobody called?
It's cold in here, isn't it?
entries.русский: не является, не (сокращение от is not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.question form: Isn't he coming? — the contraction inverts as one word, in front of the subject. ✗ Is not he coming? is not English, and Is he not coming? is formal and emphatic.
entries.contrast: Two syllables: the -n't is a syllabic /ənt/, IZ-uhnt. And He isn't ready and He's not ready say the same thing — the second puts the weight on not. Both are standard.

examples: These aren't my keys.
Aren't you cold in that jacket?
We aren't going to make it on time.
I'm on the list too, aren't I?
Aren't I supposed to sign this part?

senses.head: The contraction of are not
examples: These aren't my keys.
Aren't you cold in that jacket?
We aren't going to make it on time.

senses.head: In the first-person question, the contraction of am not
examples: I'm on the list too, aren't I?
Aren't I supposed to sign this part?

entries.русский: не являются, не (сокращение от are not; в вопросе aren't I? — от am not)
entries.expands to: are not — and, in the question aren't I?, am not
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.ambiguity: Nearly always are not. Only in the first-person question does it stand for am not: I'm late, aren't I? The statement stays I'm not late — never ✗ I aren't late.
entries.question form: The first-person tag is aren't I?, because English has no amn't. Am I not? exists but is formal.
entries.contrast: One syllable, ARNT — the -n't adds no extra syllable here, unlike the two-syllable isn't and wasn't. Keep it apart from the nonstandard ain't /eɪnt/, which is a different word entirely.

examples: It wasn't my fault.
She wasn't home when I called.
That wasn't what I meant to say.
entries.русский: не был, не была, не было (сокращение от was not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: wasn't goes with I, he, she and it; after you, we and they it is weren't.

examples: They weren't expecting us.
Weren't you supposed to call me?
If it weren't so late, I'd stay for another coffee.
entries.русский: не были (сокращение от were not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: One syllable, WURNT — unlike most of these, there is no -uhnt. In the unreal conditional the verb is were for every subject, so the negative is weren't: If I weren't so tired, I'd come. If I wasn't is common in speech and avoided in writing.

entries.meaning: The contraction of do not — the ordinary negative of the present tense and of the imperative. ---
examples: I don't know what happened.
Don't touch that — it's hot.
We don't have to leave yet.
entries.русский: не делаю, не делают; не надо (сокращение от do not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.question form: Don't you like it? — one word in front of the subject. ✗ Do not you like it? is not English; Do you not like it? is formal.
entries.contrast: One syllable, /doʊnt/, rhyming with won't. Use it with I, you, we and they; with he, she and it the form is doesn't. He don't care is everywhere in speech and song and still counts as an error in writing.

examples: He doesn't speak Spanish.
It doesn't matter now.
Doesn't the store close at nine?
entries.русский: не делает (сокращение от does not, 3-е лицо ед. ч.)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.question form: Doesn't she know? — the contraction inverts as one word, and the main verb stays bare: ✗ Doesn't she knows?
entries.contrast: Spelled from does, but said with the vowel of was: DUZ-uhnt, never 'DOZE-uhnt'. The verb after it loses its -s: She doesn't work here, not ✗ She doesn't works here.

entries.meaning: The contraction of did not — the negative of the simple past. ---
examples: I didn't see your message.
We didn't mean to wake you.
Didn't you get my email?
entries.русский: не делал, не сделал (сокращение от did not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: The past is already marked in didn't, so the verb that follows stays in its bare form: I didn't go, never ✗ I didn't went.

examples: I haven't finished the report yet.
We haven't seen each other since college.
Haven't you heard the news?
entries.русский: не имею, не имеют; ещё не (сокращение от have not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: As an auxiliary it makes the negative perfect: I haven't finished. For possession, American English says I don't have a car; I haven't got a car is understood but sounds British.

examples: She hasn't called me back.
The package hasn't arrived yet.
Hasn't he told you already?
entries.русский: не имеет; ещё не (сокращение от has not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: He's gone has two negatives: He hasn't gone and He's not gone. Both are standard, and the second stresses the not.

entries.meaning: The contraction of had not — the negative of the past perfect. ---
examples: I hadn't met her before that evening.
If we hadn't left early, we'd have missed the flight.
He said he hadn't heard anything about it.
entries.русский: не имел; ещё не (сокращение от had not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: The negative of had better is had better not, never ✗ hadn't better: You'd better not be late.

examples: I won't be at the meeting on Thursday.
The car won't start in this cold.
She won't answer her phone.
entries.русский: не буду, не будет; не хочет (сокращение от will not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.question form: Won't you sit down? — the contracted question is the natural one; Will you not sit down? is stiff and marked.
entries.contrast: The sound has nothing of will in it: /woʊnt/, one syllable, rhyming with don't, not 'will-not' run together. Keep it apart from want /wɑːnt/ — He won't eat and He wants to eat are opposites.

examples: I wouldn't do that if I were you.
The door wouldn't open.
She said she wouldn't be late.
entries.русский: не стал бы, не хотел (сокращение от would not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: The l is silent and the -n't is a syllabic /ənt/: WOOD-uhnt, two syllables. In fast speech the final t is barely there, so it can sound like wooden with something after it.

examples: I can't hear you — there's too much noise.
We can't afford that right now.
Can't you come a little earlier?
entries.русский: не могу, не может; нельзя (сокращение от cannot)
entries.expands to: cannot — that is, can plus not
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.question form: Can't you hear me? — one word in front of the subject. ✗ Cannot you hear me? is not English; the formal version is Can you not hear me?
entries.contrast: American /kænt/ rhymes with ant; the British /kɑːnt/ is the other vowel. In American speech the real difference between can and can't is not the final t, which often becomes a catch in the throat, but the vowel: I can go reduces can to /kən/, while can't keeps its full vowel and takes the stress.

entries.meaning: The negative of can, written as one word. ---
examples: I cannot accept these terms.
The committee cannot meet before Friday.
Applicants who cannot attend in person may send a representative.
entries.русский: не могу, не может; нельзя (can + not, пишется слитно)
entries.expands to: can not, written solid as one word
entries.type: negative — one word, and not a contraction: it is simply how can plus not is written
entries.register: standard — the full written form; can't is the everyday spoken one
entries.question form: There is no question form. The question is Can't you…?, or the formal Can you not…?; ✗ Cannot you…? is not English.
entries.contrast: Write it solid. Two words, can not, is correct only when the not belongs to what follows: You can not only sing but also dance. Everywhere else ✗ I can not swim is an error for I cannot swim. Of the modals, only can does this — will not and should not stay two words.

examples: I couldn't find your house.
We couldn't believe our eyes.
Couldn't you have told me earlier?
entries.русский: не мог, не смог; не мог бы (сокращение от could not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: The l is silent: KOOD-uhnt. The idiom is I couldn't care less; Americans say I could care less constantly and mean the same thing, but it is illogical and gets corrected in writing.

examples: You shouldn't work so late.
I shouldn't have said that.
Shouldn't we ask first?
entries.русский: не следует, не должен (сокращение от should not)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: shouldn't plus a past participle is a reproach or a regret about something already done: You shouldn't have told him. It is also the everyday American replacement for oughtn't and, in prohibitions, for mustn't.

entries.meaning: The contraction of must not — a prohibition, not a lack of obligation. ---
examples: You mustn't say anything to your sister.
We mustn't lose this chance.
Visitors mustn't feed the animals.
entries.русский: нельзя, не должен (сокращение от must not; запрет)
entries.register: standard — correct, but uncommon in American English, which says can't, don't or not allowed to
entries.question form: Americans do not ask Mustn't we? The question is Don't we have to? or Can't we?
entries.contrast: The first t is silent: MUS-uhnt. And mustn't and don't have to are opposites — You mustn't tell her forbids it, You don't have to tell her leaves it up to you. American English usually reaches for can't instead: You can't tell her.

entries.meaning: The contraction of shall not — rare in American English. ---
examples: 'I shan't be a moment,' she called from the hallway.
We shan't be seeing them again this summer.
He shan't have the satisfaction of hearing me complain.
entries.русский: не буду (сокращение от shall not; британское и устаревшее)
entries.register: dated — British and old-fashioned; in American English use won't
entries.question form: There is no American question form. Shan't we? is British; the American tag is Won't we?, and the offer is Shall we? with no negative at all.
entries.contrast: In American English shall itself has almost disappeared outside Shall we? and legal writing, so shan't reads as a quotation, a period piece or a joke. Say won't. British /ʃɑːnt/, American /ʃænt/ on the rare occasions it is said.

entries.meaning: The contraction of need not — it is not necessary. ---
examples: You needn't wait for me.
We needn't have hurried — the train was late.
She needn't know about any of this.
entries.русский: не нужно, не обязательно (сокращение от need not)
entries.register: standard — correct but formal and uncommon in American English, which says don't need to or don't have to
entries.question form: Americans do not ask Needn't we? The question is Don't we need to?
entries.contrast: Semi-modal, so the verb after it is a bare infinitive: You needn't wait, never ✗ You needn't to wait. Used as an ordinary verb, need takes to and the do forms instead: You don't need to wait.

entries.meaning: The contraction of ought not — rare in American English. ---
examples: You oughtn't to speak to her like that.
We oughtn't to have left him alone.
Oughtn't somebody to tell him?
entries.русский: не следует (сокращение от ought not)
entries.register: dated — rare in American English, which says shouldn't
entries.question form: Oughtn't we? sounds British and bookish; the American tag is Shouldn't we?
entries.contrast: ought keeps to before the verb: You oughtn't to say that, not ✗ You oughtn't say that — though the to is often dropped in speech, which is one more reason Americans simply say You shouldn't say that.

entries.meaning: The contraction of dare not — to lack the nerve to do something. ---
examples: I daren't tell him what it cost.
She daren't look down.
We daren't move until the noise stopped.
entries.русский: не смею, не осмеливается (сокращение от dare not)
entries.register: dated — chiefly British and literary; American English says doesn't dare
entries.question form: Daren't we? does not occur in American English; the question is Do we dare?
entries.contrast: Semi-modal, so a bare infinitive follows and there is no -s in the third person: She daren't ask, never ✗ She daren't to ask or ✗ She daren'ts ask. The ordinary American sentence is She doesn't dare ask or She doesn't dare to ask.

entries.meaning: The contraction of might not — rare in American English. ---
examples: Mightn't it be better to wait?
She mightn't have heard you.
I thought you mightn't come.
entries.русский: может не, вряд ли (сокращение от might not)
entries.register: dated — chiefly British; American English writes the two words might not
entries.question form: Mightn't it be simpler to ask? is British. An American asks Wouldn't it be simpler to ask? — and there is no ✗ mayn't in any variety.
entries.contrast: American English leaves might not uncontracted: He might not come. Note the meaning too — mightn't is uncertainty, not prohibition; mustn't is the prohibition.

examples: I ain't going anywhere.
That ain't what I heard.
They ain't from around here.
You ain't seen nothing yet.
He ain't finished yet.
I ain't had a day off in weeks.

senses.head: The contraction of am not, is not or are not
examples: I ain't going anywhere.
That ain't what I heard.
They ain't from around here.

senses.head: The contraction of has not or have not, before a past participle
examples: You ain't seen nothing yet.
He ain't finished yet.
I ain't had a day off in weeks.

entries.русский: не есть, не является; не имеет (просторечное сокращение от am/is/are/has/have not)
entries.expands to: am not, is not, are not, has not or have not
entries.type: negative — be or have plus not
entries.register: nonstandard — everywhere in speech, song and dialogue, and marked as an error in school and in any formal writing
entries.ambiguity: One form for five. With a subject alone it is be: I ain't is am not, he ain't is is not, they ain't is are not. Before a past participle it is have: He ain't finished is hasn't finished. Only the rest of the sentence tells you which.
entries.question form: Ain't I? and Ain't he? both occur in speech; the standard equivalents are Aren't I? and Isn't he?
entries.contrast: Recognize it; do not write it. In an essay, an email to a stranger or an exam it will be counted wrong, while in song lyrics, dialogue and everyday talk it is completely ordinary. It also travels with a second negative — I ain't got no money — where standard English has I don't have any money. The library also lists the fixed expressions ain't no, ain't nobody and ain't that the truth.
